sections.heading: Emerging technology
paragraphs: Technology applies knowledge, methods and tools to solve problems or meet needs. An emerging technology may be new or a developing form of an existing technology that is expected to create significant social or economic effects. ‘Emerging’ is time- and context-dependent: a technology can mature, change or be replaced.

Technological evolution describes how technologies and societies transform over time. Technology can change work, communication and institutions, but its effects depend on how people, organizations and governments develop and use it.

sections.heading: Industrial revolutions
bullets: Industry 1.0: mechanization, water and steam power, machine tools and the factory system replaced much hand production.
Industry 2.0: electricity, railways, telegraph networks, interchangeable parts and assembly-line mass production expanded manufacturing and communication.
Industry 3.0: electronics, computers, digital logic, automation and the Internet enabled digital control and information processing.
Industry 4.0: connected cyber-physical systems combine sensors, networks, data, robotics, AI and automation so physical processes can be monitored and coordinated digitally.
The stages overlap; each builds on earlier infrastructure and changes production, work, skills and social relationships.

sections.heading: Data, programmable devices and human-machine interaction
bullets: Data supports emerging technologies by providing observations that can be stored, processed and used for decisions, automation or learning. Data quality, context and responsible use affect the value of a system.
Programmable devices execute instructions to sense, process, store or communicate information. Examples include computers, smartphones, microcontrollers, sensors and embedded systems.

Human-computer interaction (HCI) studies how people interact with computer-based systems. It draws on computing, design, psychology and related fields to make interfaces usable, understandable, accessible and safe.
Good interaction design considers users, tasks, context, feedback, error prevention, accessibility and privacy—not just the device’s technical capability.
Future technology trends described in the module include AI, IoT, big data, cloud computing, AR/VR, robotics and automation. The chapter’s examples are a course snapshot, not a current ranking.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Compare the four industrial revolutions by their central technologies and changes to production.
Explain how programmable devices, networks and data enable emerging technologies.
Define HCI and name disciplines that contribute to user-friendly systems.

units.title: Chapter 2 - Data Science and Big Data

topics.title: Data science, data types and the data value chain

sections.heading: Data and information
bullets: Data are recorded observations or values; information is data organized and interpreted to answer a question or support understanding. Context determines whether data are meaningful.
Data science combines methods from statistics, computing and subject areas to collect, prepare, analyze and communicate findings from data.
A typical data-processing cycle includes defining a question, acquiring data, cleaning and preparing it, analyzing it, interpreting results, communicating findings and using them to guide action.

sections.heading: Types and representation
bullets: Programming types include integers, floating-point numbers, characters, strings and Boolean values; type determines representation and valid operations.
Analytics often distinguishes categorical data (labels or groups) from numerical data. Numerical data may be discrete counts or continuous measurements.
Structured data follow a defined format such as rows and columns; semi-structured data have tags or flexible organization; unstructured data include free text, images, audio and video.
Data representation affects which storage, processing and analysis methods are suitable. Poor coding, missing values, inconsistent units or biased sampling can distort conclusions.

sections.heading: Data value chain
bullets: Acquisition gathers data from sources such as surveys, transactions, sensors, records or public datasets, with attention to consent, relevance and quality.
Curation organizes, documents, cleans and maintains data so they are usable and traceable.
Storage keeps data in appropriate systems with access controls, backup, security and retention policies.
Analysis applies descriptive, diagnostic, predictive or other methods to answer defined questions.
Usage turns analysis into decisions, services or products. Communicating uncertainty and limitations is part of responsible use.

sections.heading: Big data and clustered computing
bullets: Big data refers to datasets whose scale, speed, diversity or complexity can exceed the practical capacity of traditional tools. Common descriptions include volume, velocity and variety; veracity and value are also often considered.
Clustered computing uses multiple connected computers to divide storage or processing tasks. Distributed work can improve scale and throughput but adds coordination and fault-management challenges.

Hadoop is an ecosystem for distributed storage and processing. HDFS distributes files across machines; MapReduce divides computation into map and reduce stages; related tools support data management and analysis.
A big-data workflow includes ingestion, distributed storage, processing, analysis and output. The architecture should fit the problem; not every dataset needs a big-data platform.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Distinguish data from information and explain the stages of the data value chain.
Compare structured, semi-structured and unstructured data with examples.
Explain why distributed computing is used and identify one trade-off of using a cluster.

topics.title: AI concepts, history, levels and types

sections.heading: What AI studies
paragraphs: Artificial intelligence (AI) is the study and development of computer systems that perform tasks associated with abilities such as perception, language, learning, reasoning, planning and decision-making. AI systems carry out specific computational tasks; their operation should not be confused with human understanding or consciousness.

sections.heading: Goals, history and categories
bullets: AI research aims to build systems that perceive environments, represent or learn from information, reason about alternatives and take actions toward goals.

The history of AI includes early symbolic reasoning, periods of reduced investment when expectations exceeded results, and later progress supported by more data, computing power and improved algorithms.
Narrow or weak AI is designed for specific tasks. General or strong AI describes a broader human-level capability and remains a theoretical goal rather than a capability of ordinary current systems.

AI can be classified by capability (narrow versus general) or by approach (systems that imitate human thought or behavior versus systems that act rationally toward goals). These classification schemes answer different questions.

Machine learning is a major AI approach in which systems learn patterns from examples rather than relying only on hand-written rules. Deep learning uses multilayer neural networks and often benefits from large datasets and computing resources.

sections.heading: Influencers and applications
bullets: Big data supplies examples; data science provides methods to prepare and analyze them; cloud computing offers scalable storage and processing; APIs let software services exchange functions or data.
AI applications include language tools, image recognition, recommendation, decision support and automation in fields such as health, education, agriculture and business.
An AI tool is appropriate only when it fits the task, data, users and risks. Performance should be checked with relevant measures and representative cases.
A typical AI workflow defines a task, gathers and prepares data, selects or trains a model, evaluates it, deploys it and monitors performance over time.

sections.heading: Benefits, limits and exam review
bullets: AI can process information quickly, automate repetitive tasks, identify patterns and support decisions. It can also make errors, reflect biased data, reduce transparency, affect jobs or create privacy and security concerns.
AI output is not automatically accurate or fair. Human review, clear accountability, suitable data and ongoing evaluation are important, especially when decisions affect people.
Distinguish AI, machine learning and deep learning: machine learning is a set of methods within AI; deep learning is a subset of machine learning.
For an application question, identify the task, input data, model output, benefit, limitation and who is responsible for the decision.

sections.heading: What is IoT
paragraphs: The Internet of Things (IoT) connects physical objects equipped with sensors, software or actuators to networks so they can collect, exchange and sometimes act on data. The object, network, data service and user or control system work together.

sections.heading: How IoT systems work
bullets: A sensor measures a physical condition such as temperature, location, motion or moisture. A device processes or transmits the measurement; a network carries data to a gateway, edge system or cloud service; software analyzes it; an actuator or user may respond.

A simplified architecture includes perception/device layer (sensing and actuation), network/communication layer, and application/service layer. Some models add processing, security and management functions across layers.
IoT devices may use wired or wireless communication such as Wi-Fi, cellular, Bluetooth, Zigbee or low-power wide-area networks, depending on range, bandwidth, power and cost.
Edge computing processes some data near the device to reduce delay or network use; cloud services provide remote storage, computing and coordination.
Interoperability requires compatible devices, protocols, data formats and services. Systems also need device identity, updates and lifecycle management.

sections.heading: Benefits, challenges and domains
bullets: IoT can support monitoring, automation, efficiency and new services in smart homes, cities, grids, farms, health and industry.
Challenges include privacy, cybersecurity, unreliable connectivity, power limits, device maintenance, data quality, interoperability, cost and unequal access.
A smart-home system may automate lighting or monitor energy; smart-city deployments may manage traffic or infrastructure; smart farming can use soil or weather data to guide irrigation.
Collect only necessary data, secure devices and communications, control access, update software and plan what happens when connectivity fails.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Trace data from sensor to network, analysis and action in an IoT example.
Explain the roles of device, network and application layers.
Evaluate one IoT benefit alongside privacy, security or reliability risks.

units.title: Chapter 5 - Augmented, Virtual and Mixed Reality

sections.heading: AR, VR and MR
bullets: Virtual reality (VR) places the user in a computer-generated environment, often blocking or replacing the view of the physical world.
Augmented reality (AR) overlays digital information or objects on a view of the real world, commonly through a phone, tablet, headset or projection.
Mixed reality (MR) describes experiences in which digital and physical objects are presented together and may interact or be spatially anchored. Terminology can vary across products and fields.
The reality-virtuality continuum ranges from the physical environment through augmented reality and mixed forms toward fully virtual environments.

sections.heading: How augmented reality works
bullets: An AR system captures information about the scene using a camera or sensors, identifies features or markers, estimates device position and orientation, renders digital content and aligns it with the user’s view.
A typical architecture includes input and sensing, tracking or registration, processing and content, display, and user interaction.
Registration is the alignment of virtual content with the real scene. Poor tracking, lighting, calibration or latency can make overlays drift or appear unstable.
Displays may be handheld, head-mounted or spatial. Each has trade-offs in field of view, comfort, visibility, cost and interaction.

sections.heading: Applications, benefits and limitations
bullets: AR/MR can support education, training, maintenance, navigation, design, medicine and entertainment by placing relevant information in context.
VR can support simulation and immersive practice where a controlled environment is useful; AR can preserve awareness of surroundings while adding information.
Limitations include hardware cost, battery life, motion discomfort, accessibility, visual clutter, privacy from cameras and sensors, safety in shared spaces and the need for accurate content.
Choose the technology based on the learning or work task, user context and safety—not novelty alone.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Compare AR, VR and MR and place them on the reality-virtuality continuum.
Describe the sensing, tracking, rendering and display stages of an AR system.
Give one suitable use and one limitation for AR and VR.

units.title: Chapter 6 - Emerging Technology, Ethics and Society

sections.heading: Ethical questions
bullets: Technology ethics examines how design and use affect people, communities and the environment. Consider who benefits, who may be harmed, who is excluded and who has power over a system.
Privacy concerns what personal information is collected, why it is collected, how long it is kept, who can access it and whether people have meaningful choices.
Accountability requires clear responsibility for system design, deployment, decisions, errors and correction. Automation does not remove human or organizational responsibility.
Trust depends on reliable performance, understandable limits, secure handling of information, fair treatment and honest communication about how a system works.
Bias can enter through data collection, labels, model choices, evaluation or deployment context. Test systems across relevant groups and provide ways to challenge harmful outcomes.

sections.heading: Responsible technology practices
bullets: Use data for a defined and legitimate purpose, collect only what is needed, protect it and set clear retention and deletion rules.
Explain automated decisions in a way suitable for affected users; provide human review where decisions carry significant consequences.
Assess accessibility, safety, environmental costs, security and unintended uses before deployment and monitor them afterward.
Use informed participation and consultation when a system affects communities; include people with different needs and perspectives in design and evaluation.

sections.heading: Threats and challenges
bullets: Threats include cyberattacks, surveillance, data misuse, misinformation, unsafe automation, unequal access, job disruption and dependence on fragile infrastructure.
A balanced assessment compares likely benefits, possible harms, likelihood, severity, affected groups and available safeguards.
Ethical principles should be translated into design choices, policies, testing, governance and procedures for reporting and correcting problems.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Distinguish privacy from security and explain how they relate.
Apply accountability and fairness questions to an AI or IoT example.
Describe safeguards that could reduce a technology’s risks while preserving its useful benefits.

sections.heading: Nanotechnology and biotechnology
bullets: Nanotechnology works with materials and structures at very small scales, where properties can differ from bulk materials. Potential uses include electronics, materials, medicine and energy; safety and environmental effects need assessment.
Biotechnology applies biological systems, organisms or processes to develop products and services, including applications in health, agriculture, industry and environmental management.
Both fields can bring useful advances and raise questions about safety, access, environmental impact, regulation and responsible research.

sections.heading: Blockchain
bullets: A blockchain is a shared digital ledger in which transactions are grouped into linked records and validated according to a protocol across a network.
Distributed ledgers can support records that are difficult to alter without network agreement, but ‘immutable’ does not guarantee that entered information is true or that software has no flaws.
Public and permissioned systems differ in who can participate and validate. Consensus methods, performance, governance, privacy and energy use vary by design.
Possible uses include digital asset records and supply-chain tracking; suitability depends on whether shared verification is actually needed.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Define nanotechnology and biotechnology and give a possible application of each.
Explain what a blockchain records and why it cannot guarantee the accuracy of every input.
Assess a technology by considering usefulness, feasibility, safety and governance.

topics.title: Cloud and quantum computing, autonomic systems and computer vision

sections.heading: Computing approaches
bullets: Cloud computing provides on-demand access over a network to shared computing resources such as storage, servers, platforms and software. It can scale quickly but depends on connectivity, provider security and service terms.

Quantum computing uses quantum states and operations to process information in ways different from classical computing. It may help with selected classes of problems, but it is not faster for every task and remains technically challenging.
Autonomic computing aims for systems that manage themselves with limited human intervention. Common goals include self-configuration, self-healing, self-optimization and self-protection.
Embedded systems are computing units built into larger devices to perform dedicated functions, often with limits on power, memory and response time.

sections.heading: Computer vision and cybersecurity
bullets: Computer vision enables systems to derive information from images or video, for tasks such as object recognition, inspection, medical imaging and traffic monitoring.
Vision systems depend on suitable images, labels, lighting and evaluation; errors can arise from poor data, unusual conditions or bias in the examples used.

Cybersecurity protects systems, networks and data from unauthorized access, disruption or misuse. Good practice includes updates, strong access controls, backups, secure configuration and incident response.
Security is a continuing process because threats, software and connected devices change over time.

sections.heading: Additive manufacturing and final review
bullets: Additive manufacturing (3D printing) builds an object layer by layer from a digital design. It can support rapid prototyping, customization and complex shapes, while material, speed, cost, quality and scale affect production choices.
Compare additive manufacturing with subtractive or traditional processes by considering material waste, design freedom, production volume, finishing and equipment requirements.
For any emerging technology, revise its definition, how it works, likely applications, benefits, limits, ethical issues and the conditions for responsible use.

Technologies often combine: IoT devices generate data, cloud platforms store it, AI analyzes it and interfaces such as AR present results. Analyze the whole system, including its dependencies and risks.

sections.heading: Final exam quick check
bullets: Compare cloud, quantum and autonomic computing by purpose and current limitations.
Describe one computer-vision application and one risk or source of error.
Explain additive manufacturing and evaluate when it may be appropriate.
Use a consistent framework: need, mechanism, data/resources, benefit, limitation, ethics and safeguards.
